title: Building the lens, and checking it
intro: The summary gave the instrument in three equations. This level covers what building the matrix actually costs and which choices inside the recipe were tested, the three different ways the paper reads from it, the arithmetic of writing with it, the evaluations that place it against the two older lenses, and the concepts it cannot name at all.

chapters.title: The price of the matrix
chapters.body:
The matrix is built by backpropagation, and the pseudocode the paper supplies makes the cost legible.

For each prompt in the corpus, a forward pass runs and caches the residual stream at every layer and position. Then, for each of the $d_{\text{model}}$ dimensions of the target vector, a gradient of one is injected at that dimension at every position and propagated backwards. A single backward pass yields one row of the Jacobian at every layer at once, so the layers come free: cost scales with the model's width and the corpus size, not its depth [[jacobian-computation-procedure]]. The default corpus is one thousand sequences of 128 tokens each, sampled from a pretraining-like distribution [[lens-corpus]].

That expense is paid once per model. Afterwards a readout is one matrix multiplication, which places the technique at the cheap end of the activation-readout tools [[readout-method-tradeoffs]].

Three choices sit inside the recipe [[j-lens-recipe-variants]]. The first is where the backward pass starts. The default differentiates the penultimate layer rather than the final one, because the last block is heavily specialized for calibrating next-token predictions, and including it can add noisy artifacts to readouts [[target-layer-choice]]. The second is which pathways the gradient may use: a frozen-QK variant zeroes gradients through the query and key projections, holding the attention pattern fixed so that only the value pathway contributes [[frozen-qk-variant]]. A related choice sets which output positions are targeted, all $t' \geq t$ by default, or the source position alone, or strictly later positions alone [[target-position-variants]]. The third is the estimator, per-element mean or median across prompts, with outliers optionally filtered out [[jacobian-aggregation]].

The paper reports that these choices matter little. Across five recipes crossed with both estimators, intermediate extraction and causal effect stay fairly consistent, with the penultimate-layer mean slightly ahead on extraction and frozen QK slightly ahead on causal effect [[fig-57]]. Sweeping the corpus from one prompt to a thousand, the lens beats both baselines with as few as ten prompts, and further data buys modest gains [[fig-59]].

One approximation underlies all of it: the layers above $\ell$ are treated as locally linear [[local-linearization]].

chapters.title: Three ways of reading one activation
chapters.body:
The same matrix is read in three ways, answering different questions.

The first is the ranked list: score every vocabulary token, sort, print the top few [[j-lens-readout]]. The second drops the ranking. The pre-softmax logits are determined, up to a data-dependent normalization factor, by the inner products of the activation with each lens vector, so one chosen vector can serve as a probe: the score of $h_\ell$ against that direction, compared to a threshold [[j-lens-probe]]. It is the form used when the paper asks whether one specific concept is present.

The third is sparse decomposition, and it asks which small set of directions actually reconstructs the activation [[sparse-decomposition]]. The paper solves for a nonnegative combination of $k$ lens vectors by gradient pursuit, a greedy sparse-approximation algorithm [[gradient-pursuit]]. Because the vectors are overcomplete and non-orthogonal, the set it returns is typically less redundant than the top $k$ by inner product. The value of $k$ is fixed by hand, between ten and twenty-five depending on the experiment [[sparsity-level-k]]. Fixing it also turns a pile of vectors into a space: a union of cones, one for each choice of $k$ vectors [[union-of-cones]], with the nearest point in that union taken as an activation's J-space component [[j-space-component]].

A readout is not prose, and the instructions handed to an automated auditor say so: "Treat the token list as a bag of ideas, not a sentence"; "An idea can surface as many related words (synonyms, names, variants). Look for the family, not one exact term"; and an idea is more credible "if it shows up across several layers, or across several nearby token positions" [[lens-readout-reading-heuristics]].

The hedge is stated plainly. In roughly the first third of the model readouts are noisy and largely uninterpretable, and elsewhere some cells simply resist reading, which the paper records without characterizing why [[uninterpretable-readouts]]. Layer numbers run 0-100 across 25 evenly spaced layers, so they read as percentages of depth [[layer-percentage-indexing]]. The interactive viewer exists for reading across cells rather than one: a grid of top tokens over every position and layer, with rank trajectories for pinned tokens [[j-lens-visualization]], [[fig-5]].

chapters.title: Writing along the same directions
chapters.body:
Three writes are available, and each has its own arithmetic [[j-lens-interventions]].

Steering is the simplest: $h \leftarrow h + \alpha\,v_t$, applied at chosen layers and token positions [[j-lens-steering]]. With a negative $\alpha$, or by projecting out the component along $v_t$ entirely, the same move becomes an ablation of that one concept [[j-lens-ablation]]. Running that projection against the top-$k$ active vectors at every position is the wholesale version, used elsewhere in the paper to suppress the workspace as a whole [[j-space-ablation]].

The swap is more careful, because the frame is oblique. Lens vectors are neither orthogonal to one another nor unit-norm, so an inner product does not give an activation's coordinate along one of them [[oblique-lens-coordinates]]. The paper forms $V = [v_s\; v_t]$, reads the coordinates as $c = V^\dagger h$ with the pseudoinverse [[pseudoinverse]], and writes back $h_{\text{patched}} = h + V(\sigma(c) - c)$. Everything orthogonal to the span of the two vectors is left alone, and the specificity claimed for every swap result rests on that clause [[lens-coordinate-swap]].

Around the core operation sit the settings. The exchange carries a strength multiplier; at $\alpha = 2$ the source vector is subtracted and the target added at double strength [[swap-strength-alpha]]. Coordinates can also be held at fixed values at every position and layer through the whole forward pass, rather than set once [[activation-clamping]]. More than one pair can be exchanged at a time [[multi-concept-swap]]. A swap is scored not by whether the output moves but by whether it becomes the answer the prompt would have had if the swapped-in concept were the true one [[implied-counterfactual-answer]].

The last point is where the instrument's limits show. A swap that changes nothing is read as evidence that the computation does not route through the workspace. The paper also records the duller explanation, that the intervention was too weak or the vector badly chosen, which makes a null result weaker evidence than a positive one [[null-swap-interpretation]].

chapters.title: Set against the two older lenses
chapters.childScope: Take the lens comparison at full resolution: the six intermediate-concept benchmarks one at a time ([[intermediate-concept-benchmarks]], with the multihop, multilingual, order-of-operations, poetry, typo and association sets), the readout metric [[pass-at-k-auc]] and [[fig-52]], the two causal metrics [[ablation-kl-effect]] and [[swap-success-rate]] with [[fig-53]] and [[fig-54]], the next-token agreement result in [[fig-55]], and the layer-by-layer [[inter-lens-agreement]] including [[tuned-lens-bias-term]].
chapters.body:
The comparison does not rest on side-by-side readouts [[lens-evaluation]]. Six prompt distributions were assembled in which the model must compute a known intermediate that is neither in the input nor identical to the output: fifty two-hop factual questions, fifty-four prompts in a non-English language, fifty-five arithmetic expressions, fifty-two rhyming couplets, ninety-six sentences ending on a misspelling, and fifty passages that depict a concept without naming it [[intermediate-concept-benchmarks]]. Every intermediate is a single-token word, read at one fixed position per item.

Recovery is scored by pass@k, summarized as the area under that curve against $\log k$, normalized so always ranking the intermediate first scores one [[pass-at-k-auc]]. The J-lens leads on all six distributions. Its margin over the logit lens is modest on the two-hop and association sets, and substantial on the other four. The tuned lens trails both, recovering almost nothing on poetry and association, the two sets where the next token at the read position is a newline and a period [[fig-52]].

Ranking is correlational, so two causal measures follow. Projecting out each lens's direction for the intermediate and recording the induced KL divergence gives roughly twice the divergence for J-lens directions on two-hop items [[ablation-kl-effect]], [[fig-53]]. Swapping along them flips the top-1 output to the counterfactual answer more often, at all three model scales [[swap-success-rate]].

On the metric the tuned lens is trained for, agreement with the model's own next-token distribution, the J-lens is worst of the three, with higher KL than even the uncorrected logit lens through most of the network [[fig-55]]. The paper treats that as a feature, on the grounds that the directions best at anticipating the output are not the ones best at exposing the computation producing it.

A last comparison sets the lenses against each other rather than a ground truth, and the four layer ranges it picks out line up with the workspace boundaries found elsewhere [[inter-lens-agreement]], [[fig-56]]. One result there is sharp: in early layers the tuned lens's whole advantage over the logit lens comes from its learned bias, not its linear part, which is to say from ignoring the input [[tuned-lens-bias-term]].

chapters.title: The concepts the vocabulary cannot hold
chapters.childScope: Cover the instrument's coverage gap in full: [[single-token-limitation]] and the length falloff in [[fig-62]], the [[template-lens]] construction and whitening [[template-construction]] with its Stein's-lemma motivation, its results in [[fig-61]] and [[fig-63]] and its listed shortcomings, the four-stage [[oracle-training]] pipeline behind the [[oracle-lens]] including the [[reconstructor-model]], its readouts in [[fig-64]] and the [[delimiter-commentary]] split, and the [[bag-of-concepts-limitation]] that remains after both.
chapters.body:
The lens supplies one vector per vocabulary token, so a concept whose name is not a single token has no vector [[single-token-limitation]]. On the blackmail transcript the readout registers the act only as the fragments black and ext. On a two-hop item whose unspoken intermediate is photosynthesis, the best it manages is phot. Across multi-hop prompts whose intermediates run from one to four tokens, readout and swap performance both fall off sharply as it lengthens, and averaging lens scores over the word's constituent tokens does not repair it [[fig-62]].

Two extensions were built for this [[multi-token-lens-extensions]]. The template lens starts from a list of roughly 12,700 common words. For each word, Claude writes short passages that end just before the word would appear, never using it; the mean activation at that final position, centered and whitened, becomes the word's template [[template-lens]], [[template-construction]]. Stein's lemma is offered as motivation, since for Gaussian activations that expression approximates the expected gradient the J-lens computes, though activations are not Gaussian. Templates read and steer like lens vectors, hold roughly flat across intermediate lengths, and decode blackmail and photosynthesis outright [[fig-61]]. The costs are stated: a few hundred forward passes per word against one set of backward passes per layer, a vocabulary enumerated in advance, an inherited habit of skipping to the answer, and a next-word top-ten hit rate of 67%.

The oracle lens drops the fixed vocabulary at the price of two fine-tuned models: a reconstructor mapping a phrase to the activation preceding it, a dictionary of about 3.4 million phrase vectors, a matching-pursuit teacher labelling activations, then supervised training plus reinforcement learning on reconstruction reward [[oracle-lens]], [[oracle-training]]. It explains 31% of whitened activation variance on held-out assistant text, and reads out phrases, not tokens [[fig-64]]. At most positions those phrases are predicted continuations; at delimiters they often read as commentary on the situation, sometimes in the first person [[delimiter-commentary]].

Even with whole phrases, the readout stays a flat list. The paper grants that a set of active concepts says nothing about how they are bound together, and calls the picture a first approximation [[bag-of-concepts-limitation]].
